Farmer.reason: Livestock, crops, and irrigation assets are the main risk.
do: Move livestock to raised ground immediately.
Cover stored fodder and seeds with waterproof sheets.
Shift pesticides and fertilizers above flood level.
Drain water away from crop storage areas.
Keep a small emergency feed stock ready.
dont: Do not let animals drink floodwater.
Do not store grains on the floor.
Do not enter flooded fields.
Do not keep chemicals in open sheds.
Do not wait until water reaches the house.

Student.reason: Schooling, safe transport, documents, and family contact are the main concerns.
do: Stay with parents, teachers, or trusted adults.
Keep school bag, ID, and documents in a waterproof cover.
Move to higher ground if water rises nearby.
Save emergency contact numbers on your phone.
Follow school or local authority instructions immediately.
dont: Do not walk through moving floodwater.
Do not use school routes that pass through low areas.
Do not touch electric switches if water is inside.
Do not ignore school closure alerts.
Do not carry heavy bags into floodwater.

Elderly.reason: Mobility, medicines, and quick evacuation support are the main risks.
do: Keep medicines, spectacles, and walking aids within reach.
Move to a safe upper floor or raised place early.
Keep emergency phone numbers visible.
Ask a family member or neighbor to assist evacuation.
Store drinking water and light food beside the bed.
dont: Do not stay alone in a flooded area.
Do not walk in water without help.
Do not delay evacuation if water rises quickly.
Do not take medicines after they are wet or damaged.
Do not use stairs alone if visibility is poor.

Worker.reason: Commute safety, workplace equipment, and wage-loss risk are the main concerns.
do: Stop travel if roads are flooded.
Secure tools, documents, and work materials in waterproof bags.
Inform your employer or supervisor early.
Move to a safe shelter before water rises.
Keep a phone charger and cash ready.
dont: Do not drive or ride through deep water.
Do not go to work through unsafe routes.
Do not touch wet electrical equipment.
Do not continue outdoor labor in floodwater.
Do not delay reporting unsafe conditions.

Industry.reason: Machinery, chemicals, data, and worker safety are the main risks.
do: Move critical machinery and stock to higher floors.
Shut down unsafe electrical systems before water enters.
Protect documents, servers, and backup data.
Seal chemical storage areas properly.
Activate flood emergency response and evacuation plan.
dont: Do not continue operations in flooded zones.
Do not allow staff to enter waterlogged areas.
Do not store chemicals near drains or low floors.
Do not ignore backup power safety checks.
Do not restart equipment until inspection is done.

Farmer.reason: Crops, livestock shelters, and outdoor farm structures are highly exposed to wind damage.
do: Move livestock to a strong closed shelter.
Tie down or bring inside loose farm equipment.
Protect seed stock and harvested produce.
Reinforce shed doors and windows.
Keep emergency feed and water ready.
dont: Do not stay near trees, poles, or tin roofs.
Do not leave livestock outside during strong winds.
Do not use open flames if power fails.
Do not travel to the farm during peak storm time.
Do not ignore official evacuation alerts.

Student.reason: School closure, family safety, and communication are the main concerns.
do: Stay indoors with parents or guardians.
Keep school closure updates on phone or radio.
Charge your phone and power bank early.
Move away from windows and glass doors.
Keep study materials and documents dry.
dont: Do not go outside to watch the cyclone.
Do not stand near windows during strong wind.
Do not use elevators if power is unstable.
Do not ignore school or local warning messages.
Do not leave younger siblings alone.

Elderly.reason: Medical needs, stability, and caregiver support are the main risks.
do: Keep medicines and prescriptions in one safe place.
Stay in the safest inner room of the house.
Ask a family member to stay nearby.
Keep a working phone with emergency numbers.
Prepare soft food and drinking water in advance.
dont: Do not go out during the cyclone.
Do not stand near windows or weak walls.
Do not use candles if a battery torch is available.
Do not move around alone in the dark.
Do not delay reaching a safer shelter if advised.

Worker.reason: Travel disruption, workplace shutdown, and injury risk are the main concerns.
do: Leave work early if warnings increase.
Secure tools, vehicles, and materials.
Inform your supervisor about your location.
Stay away from construction sites and open areas.
Keep a backup route and shelter option ready.
dont: Do not travel in strong wind or heavy rain.
Do not work near scaffolding, poles, or glass.
Do not touch fallen wires.
Do not use unsafe transport during the storm.
Do not ignore evacuation instructions.

Industry.reason: Structural safety, staff evacuation, and equipment shutdown are the key priorities.
do: Pause operations before the cyclone peaks.
Secure roofs, doors, and external objects.
Move critical inventory to safer indoor areas.
Shut down vulnerable machinery safely.
Ensure staff evacuation and attendance tracking.
dont: Do not keep production running in unsafe conditions.
Do not leave heavy materials unsecured outdoors.
Do not allow staff to remain near glass zones.
Do not use lifts during power instability.
Do not restart operations before inspection.

Farmer.reason: Field work, livestock hydration, and crop stress are the main risks.
do: Work in the early morning or evening only.
Provide drinking water to animals regularly.
Use shade for rest breaks in the field.
Wear light cotton clothes and a cap.
Use ORS if you feel weak or dizzy.
dont: Do not work under direct sun at noon.
Do not ignore heat exhaustion symptoms.
Do not leave livestock without shade and water.
Do not wear dark or heavy clothing.
Do not skip hydration during farm work.

Student.reason: School timing, hydration, and outdoor activity limits are the main concerns.
do: Carry a water bottle and drink often.
Avoid outdoor games during peak heat hours.
Stay in shaded or cool areas during breaks.
Wear a cap and light cotton clothing.
Tell a teacher or parent if you feel unwell.
dont: Do not play outside in strong afternoon heat.
Do not ignore dizziness, headache, or nausea.
Do not wear tight or dark clothes.
Do not skip meals or water.
Do not remain in a closed hot classroom without ventilation.

Elderly.reason: Dehydration, weak heat tolerance, and medication sensitivity are the main risks.
do: Stay indoors in the coolest room available.
Drink small amounts of water often.
Keep medicines away from heat and sunlight.
Use a fan, wet cloth, or cooling towel.
Ask family members to check on you regularly.
dont: Do not go outside during peak heat hours.
Do not sit in rooms without ventilation.
Do not skip water even if you do not feel thirsty.
Do not overexert yourself physically.
Do not ignore confusion, weakness, or dizziness.

Worker.reason: Physical labor, dehydration, and heat stress are the main concerns.
do: Take regular breaks in shade or cool areas.
Drink water before, during, and after work.
Wear breathable clothes and head protection.
Reduce heavy work during peak afternoon heat.
Report heat stress symptoms immediately.
dont: Do not work long hours under the direct sun.
Do not wait until you feel thirsty to drink water.
Do not ignore cramps, dizziness, or sweating changes.
Do not wear thick protective clothing unless necessary.
Do not continue working if you feel faint.

Industry.reason: Worker safety, ventilation, and heat-related productivity loss are the main risks.
do: Adjust shifts to avoid peak heat hours.
Provide cool drinking water in work areas.
Improve ventilation and airflow indoors.
Allow extra rest breaks for workers.
Train staff to recognize heat illness early.
dont: Do not schedule heavy outdoor work at midday.
Do not ignore unsafe indoor temperatures.
Do not block airflow in enclosed spaces.
Do not skip worker hydration checks.
Do not treat heat symptoms as minor issues.
